iberia: The Iberian Peninsula is the westernmost of the three major southern European peninsulas, with the Italian and Balkan peninsulas. The Pyrenees separate it from the rest of continental Europe, and the Strait of Gibraltar divides its southern tip at Tarifa from the northwest coast of Africa. Its area is about 583,254 square kilometres, and its major rivers, the Ebro, Douro, Tagus, Guadiana and Guadalquivir, flow through wide valleys between mountain systems.

The name goes back to the River Ebro, called Ibēros in Greek and Hiberus in Latin. The Ebro Treaty of 226 BCE between Rome and Carthage set the limit of Carthaginian interest at that river. Greek geographers used Iberia for the land this side of it, and Roman writers used Hispania and Hiberia as synonyms. The modern phrase Iberian Peninsula was coined in 1823 by the French geographer Jean-Baptiste Bory de Saint-Vincent.

People of the genus Homo have lived on the peninsula for at least 1.2 million years, as remains at the Atapuerca sites show. Around 2800 to 2700 BCE the Beaker culture probably arose among copper-using communities of the Tagus estuary and spread through western Europe. Bronze Age cultures such as Los Millares and El Argar developed from about 1800 BCE. By the Iron Age the peninsula held Celtic and pre-Celtic peoples, the Iberians of the east and south, and the Aquitanian cultures in the west of the Pyrenees. Phoenician merchants from Tyre founded the trading colony of Gadir, and they traded with the metal-rich community known as Tartessos.

Roman troops first occupied the peninsula in 218 BCE, during the Second Punic War against the Carthaginians, and after 197 BCE the Romans divided the Mediterranean coast and the Guadalquivir valley into Hispania Ulterior and Hispania Citerior. Celtiberian and Lusitanian resistance led to wars in the 2nd century BCE. In the early 5th century the Suebi, Vandals and Alans occupied the peninsula, and the Visigoths then took all of it, absorbing the Suebi kingdom in 584–585. Umayyad conquest followed.

In the 15th and 16th centuries Iberian expansion began a new age. The Portuguese established routes to Asia, and Spain created a vast empire in the Americas, with Seville at the centre of the transatlantic bullion trade. Jews and Moriscos were banished, and roughly 300,000 Moriscos were expelled from Spain in 1609–1614.

The peninsula is divided between most of Spain and Portugal, the microstate of Andorra, the British territory of Gibraltar and a small part of France. Its population is roughly 53 million, and its largest cities are Madrid, Barcelona and Lisbon. Apart from Basque, which is of unknown origin, all its languages descend from Vulgar Latin.
ibn-battuta: All that is known of Ibn Battuta's life comes from the account of his travels. It records that he was of Arabised Berber descent and was born into a family of Islamic legal scholars, known as qadis, in Tangier on 24 February 1304, under the Marinid dynasty. His family belonged to a Berber clan called the Lawata. As a young man he probably studied at a Sunni Maliki school, the dominant form of education in North Africa at the time.

On 14 June 1325, aged 21, he set out from Tangier on the hajj to Mecca, a journey that would ordinarily take sixteen months. He did not return to Morocco for 24 years. He travelled overland along the North African coast through Tlemcen, Béjaïa and Tunis, usually joining a caravan for safety, and reached Alexandria in the early spring of 1326. After his third pilgrimage to Mecca he decided to seek employment with Muhammad bin Tughluq, the Sultan of Delhi, and went by way of Anatolia, where members of the fityan associations of young artisans welcomed him in more than 25 towns.

He left Quanzhou in 1346 and reached Damascus in 1348, where he learned that his father had died 15 years earlier. He saw the Black Death in Syria, Palestine and Egypt, and he was back in Tangier in 1349, only to find that his mother had also died. In 1350 he went to al-Andalus, and in 1352 he crossed the Sahara by caravan from Sijilmasa, by way of the salt mines of Taghaza, to Oualata, which had recently become part of the Mali Empire.

After he came home in 1354, the Marinid ruler Abu Inan Faris suggested that he dictate an account of his journeys, which he did in Arabic to the scholar Ibn Juzayy. It is known as the Rihla and is the only source for his travels. He seems to have kept no notes, and Ibn Juzayy copied descriptions of Damascus, Mecca, Medina and Palestine from earlier travellers without acknowledging them. Modern scholars doubt that Ibn Battuta visited every place he describes. In 2010 Tim Mackintosh-Smith reported manuscripts of Islamic law at Al-Azhar University copied by Ibn Battuta in Damascus in 1326, which support the Rihla's date for his stay in Syria.
ibn-khaldun: Abd al-Rahman ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332 into an upper-class Andalusian family of Yemeni Arab descent, the Banu Khaldun, whose eponymous ancestor had settled first in Carmona and then in Seville. His first and most influential teacher was his father, under whom he studied the Islamic and the rational sciences. He also learned from Moroccan and Tunisian scholars and from Andalusian exiles in Tunis, studying Quranic recitation, Maliki law, hadith and poetry, and while still young he became a hafiz. His autobiography is described as the most detailed in medieval Muslim literature, though it lacks many personal details.

At 20 Ibn Khaldun began his political career in the chancellery of the Tunisian ruler Ibn Tafrakin as seal-bearer. Unhappy with this politically meaningless position, he followed his teacher al-Abili to Fez, where the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Fares I made him a writer of royal proclamations. He schemed against his employer and in 1357 received a prison sentence of 22 months, which ended with Abu Inan's death in 1358. He travelled through Fez, Granada and Tlemcen, repeatedly changing roles, and arrived in Cairo in 1380.

In 1384 the sultan Barquq made him professor of the Qamhiyyah Madrasah and grand qadi of the Maliki school. His efforts to reform abuses in the administration of justice met resistance, and within a year he resigned. A ship carrying his wife and children sank off Alexandria that year. He was called to the Maliki judgeship six times and never held it long.

His best-known book is the Muqaddimah, the Introduction, which he says he wrote in six months. It is the first book of the Kitab al-Ibar, begun as a history of the Berbers and expanded into a universal history in seven books. He departed from the classical style of Arab historians by synthesising multiple, sometimes contradictory sources without citations. His method had very few followers in his own time, but Ottoman historians such as Katip Celebi took up his theory of the rise and fall of empires in the 17th century. Europe first learned of him in 1697 through a biography in d'Herbelot's Bibliothèque Orientale, and the complete Arabic edition of the Muqaddimah appeared in 1858.
iliad: The Iliad is one of two major surviving ancient Greek epic poems attributed to Homer, the other being the Odyssey. It is divided into 24 books, is written in dactylic hexameter and has 15,693 lines in its standard edition. It was likely composed in Homeric Greek, a literary mixture of Ionic Greek and other dialects, in the late 8th or early 7th century BCE, and its reflection in art and literature shows that it existed before 630 BCE. Its composition, historicity and authorship are extensively debated as the Homeric Question, as is whether the poems were composed independently and whether they survived through an oral or also a written tradition.

The poem is set towards the end of the Trojan War, a ten-year siege of Troy by a coalition of Mycenaean Greek states, and centres on Achilles, whose wrath, mēnis, the poem's first word, drives the narrative. After nine years of fighting, Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, takes the captive Chryseis, and Achilles takes Briseis. Agamemnon's refusal to return Chryseis to her father, a priest of Apollo, brings a plague on the Achaeans, and when Agamemnon seizes Briseis, Achilles withdraws from the fighting.

Patroclus then fights in Achilles's armour and is killed, and Achilles returns to battle and kills the Trojan prince Hector. The poem does not depict the fall of Troy or mention the Trojan Horse, which come from later sources. The Olympian gods aid favoured warriors and cities and intervene in personal disputes, and its themes include glory, fate and pride. In the last book Achilles and Priam share food and grief and agree a truce of twelve days for Hector's burial.

The ancient Greeks esteemed the Iliad highly and used it and the Odyssey as the basis of education. Professional reciters known as rhapsodes performed it at festivals such as the Panathenaia. By the end of the fifth century BCE both poems were widely known, and in the late fifth century it was the sign of a man of standing to be able to recite them by heart.

Later writers drew on it: Shakespeare used it as a source for Troilus and Cressida, and George Chapman published his English translation in instalments from 1598, in a long-line ballad metre that quickly became a classic of English poetry. More than 2,000 manuscripts of Homer survive.
illinois: Illinois lies in the Midwest and is one of the eight states of the Great Lakes region. Most of its western border with Missouri and Iowa is the Mississippi River, the Wabash River forms part of the eastern border with Indiana, the Ohio River marks the southern border with Kentucky, and the northeast reaches into Lake Michigan. The state lies entirely in the Interior Plains, with a small unglaciated area, the Driftless Area, in the extreme north-west, where Charles Mound, at 376 metres, is the highest natural point. The Illinois River bisects the state from north-east to south-west.

The name is the modern spelling of what early French missionaries and explorers called the Illinois Native Americans. It derives from the Miami-Illinois verb irenwe·wa, 'he speaks the regular way', which passed into Ojibwe and then French. The older explanation that it means 'men' is not supported by the Illinois language, and the spelling Illinois began to appear in the early 1670s.

American Indians of successive cultures lived along the waterways for thousands of years; the Koster Site shows 7,000 years of continuous habitation. Cahokia, the largest chiefdom and urban centre of the pre-Columbian Mississippian culture, stood near present-day Collinsville. It had more than 100 platform and burial mounds, a large plaza and a woodhenge of sacred cedar, and its Monks Mound, 30 metres high, is the largest pre-Columbian structure north of the Valley of Mexico.

The French were the first Europeans to arrive, settling near the Mississippi and Illinois rivers in the 17th-century Illinois Country of New France. After American independence in 1783 made the Mississippi the national boundary, settlers arrived from Kentucky by the Ohio River. Illinois became part of the Northwest Territory and achieved statehood in 1818. John Deere's self-scouring steel plow turned the prairie into productive farmland. In the mid-19th century the Illinois and Michigan Canal and a large railroad network made the state a transportation hub, and Chicago became the world's fastest-growing city by the late 19th century. By 1900 industrial and coal-mining jobs had attracted immigrants from Eastern and Southern Europe, and the Great Migration from the South established a large black community.

Springfield is the capital and Chicago the largest city, and the Chicago metropolitan area holds about three-quarters of the state's 12.8 million residents. Two World Heritage Sites lie in Illinois: the Cahokia Mounds and part of the Wright architecture site. Illinois honours Abraham Lincoln with its slogan Land of Lincoln, and the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum is in Springfield.
immanuel-kant: Immanuel Kant was born Emanuel on 22 April 1724 in Königsberg, East Prussia, into a Lutheran family. His father, Johann Georg Kant, was a harness-maker from Memel, and his mother was Anna Regina Reuter. He was the fourth of nine children, six of whom reached adulthood. The household stressed Pietist values of religious devotion, humility and a literal reading of the Bible, and his early schooling was strict, with an emphasis on Latin and religious instruction. He changed the spelling of his name to Immanuel after learning Hebrew.

Kant received a licence to lecture at Königsberg in 1755 and taught mathematics, physics, logic and metaphysics. In 1757 he began lecturing on geography, one of the first to teach it as a subject of its own. His Universal Natural History and Theory of the Heavens (1755) set out the nebular hypothesis, in which the Solar System formed from a cloud of gas. He also suggested that other distant nebulae might be other galaxies. In 1756 he published three papers on the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, among the first systematic attempts to explain earthquakes in natural terms. He became a professor in 1770.

The Critique of Pure Reason appeared in 1781, with a heavily revised second edition in 1787. The Critique of Practical Reason followed in 1788 and the Critique of the Power of Judgment in 1790. In 1792 the King's censorship commission opposed the publication of part of his work on religion. He published the book through the University of Jena, which earned him a royal reprimand, and a royal order later required him never to publish or speak publicly about religion. He died in Königsberg on 12 February 1804, saying Es ist gut, 'It is good'.

In the Critique of Pure Reason Kant argues for transcendental idealism: space and time are forms of intuition that structure all experience, and we know only appearances, not things in themselves. He compared this to a Copernican Revolution, proposing that objects of experience conform to the mind's forms of intuition and categories, not the reverse. His aim was to secure both knowledge and morality against scepticism and determinism, and he wrote that he had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith.
india: Modern humans reached the Indian subcontinent from Africa by about 55,000 years ago. Neolithic and chalcolithic cultures arose around Mehrgarh after 7000 BCE and gradually evolved into the Indus Valley Civilisation, which flourished during 2500 to 1900 BCE around cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and Dholavira. Between 1500 and 1200 BCE an archaic form of Sanskrit diffused into India from the northwest, and its evidence is found in the Rig Veda. By the middle of the first millennium BCE caste, or varna, had emerged in the cities of the central Ganges plain, and Jainism and Buddhism arose, both stressing non-violence and rejecting birth into a fixed hereditary varna.

The Maurya Empire followed, and under Ashoka (ca. 268 to 232 BCE) it briefly controlled the major urban hubs of the subcontinent, except in the deep south. Early in the 2nd millennium Muslim armies from Central Asia intermittently overran the northern plains, eventually establishing the Delhi Sultanate. Sikhism emerged in the Punjab, and the Mughal Empire brought two centuries of economic expansion and relative peace. The British East India Company consolidated territorial control, and crown rule, the British Raj, began in 1858. A nationalist movement, noted for nonviolent resistance after 1920, was a major factor in ending British rule. In 1947 the British Indian Empire was partitioned into the dominions of India and Pakistan, a partition that brought large-scale loss of life and unprecedented migration.

The Constitution of India, drafted between 1946 and 1949, took effect on 26 January 1950 and made India a federal republic with a democratic parliamentary system. It makes untouchability illegal. The Lok Sabha, the lower house, has 543 elected members. The reorganisation of states in 1956 followed linguistic lines. India's population was 361 million in 1951. Economic reforms of the 1990s reopened the economy to the world. India has 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
indian-ocean: The Indian Ocean covers 70,560,000 km2, about 20% of the water area of the Earth's surface, with an average depth of 3,741 m. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west and Australia to the east, and to the south by the Southern Ocean or Antarctica, depending on the definition in use. Its large marginal seas include the Andaman Sea, the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and the Laccadive Sea. In 1953 the International Hydrographic Organization drew its borders to include the Southern Ocean; in 2002 it delimited the Southern Ocean separately.

Unlike the Atlantic and Pacific, the Indian Ocean is enclosed by major landmasses on three sides and does not stretch from pole to pole. Its climate is governed by the monsoon, the strongest on Earth. Strong north-east winds blow from October until April, and from May until October south and west winds prevail. The monsoon reverses the large seasonal currents, including the Somali Current.

The Indian Ocean, together with the Mediterranean, has connected people since ancient times, whereas the Atlantic and Pacific long acted as barriers. The ocean is named after India, which projects into it, and has been known by its present name since at least 1515, when the Latin form Oceanus Orientalis Indicus is attested. Ancient Greek geography called the part known to the Greeks the Erythraean Sea. Chinese explorers of the 15th century, such as Zheng He of the Ming dynasty, called it the Western Oceans.

The written history of the ocean has been largely Eurocentric, because it depends on the sources of the European colonial era. It is often divided into an ancient period and an Islamic period, followed by Portuguese, Dutch, French and British periods. A concept of an Indian Ocean World, based on the monsoon that linked Asia, China, India and Mesopotamia, is sometimes called the first global economy. It developed independently of European trade in the Mediterranean and Atlantic and remained largely independent of it until the colonial dominance of the 19th century. The first human settlement around its shores dates to the Pleistocene, with fossils of Homo erectus found in India.
indira-gandhi: Indira Nehru was born on 19 November 1917 in Allahabad, into a Kashmiri Pandit family. Her father, Jawaharlal Nehru, was a leading figure in the movement for independence from British rule. She was her parents' only surviving child and grew up with her mother, Kamala Nehru, at the Anand Bhavan estate. Her childhood was lonely: her father was often away or in prison, and her mother, frequently ill, died of tuberculosis in February 1936. She studied in India and Switzerland and at Santiniketan, founded by Rabindranath Tagore, and married Feroze Gandhi, with whom she had two sons, Rajiv and Sanjay.

In 1959, as president of the Indian National Congress, she played a part in the dissolution of the communist-led Kerala government. Lal Bahadur Shastri made her minister of information and broadcasting in 1964, and after his death in January 1966 she defeated Morarji Desai in the party's leadership election. Party bosses and the press at first called her a dumb doll, Goongi goodiya in Hindi. The Congress expelled her in 1969, and her faction, the INC (R), won a landslide in 1971 under the slogan Garibi Hatao (Remove Poverty), an answer to the opposition's Indira Hatao.

In 1969 she nationalised fourteen major commercial banks. In December 1971 India intervened in the war in East Pakistan, where the Pakistani army's repression had sent about ten million refugees across the border; it ended in Indian victory and the independence of Bangladesh. India tested a nuclear device in 1974, and Sikkim joined the Indian Union in 1975. After extending the state of emergency twice, she called elections in 1977 and lost her seat as Congress fell from 350 seats to 153. Congress returned in January 1980, and Sanjay died in a plane crash on 23 June.

In Punjab the preacher Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, whom Congress had helped to prominence, moved into a guest house near the Golden Temple in 1982 with about 200 armed followers. Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October 1984, while chairing the Non-Aligned Movement. World leaders mourned her, and Margaret Thatcher travelled to New Delhi for the funeral. She had received the Bharat Ratna in 1971, and Henry Kissinger's phrase iron lady became her nickname.
indo-european-languages: The Indo-European family is native to the north of the Indian subcontinent, most of Europe and Greater Iran, with further branches in Armenia and parts of the southern subcontinent. Historically its languages were also spoken in Anatolia and north-western China. Eight branches are still spoken: four by hundreds of millions of native speakers each (Indo-Iranian, Italic, Germanic and Balto-Slavic) and four by fewer than fifteen million each (Hellenic, Albanoid, Armenian and Celtic). Two major branches, Anatolian and Tocharian, are extinct.

Over 3.4 billion people speak an Indo-European language as a first language, the most of any language family. Ethnologue estimates about 446 living languages, of which 313 belong to the Indo-Iranian branch. Several European languages, among them English, French, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish and Dutch, spread through colonialism in the modern period.

All Indo-European languages descend from a single prehistoric language, reconstructed as Proto-Indo-European and spoken sometime in the Neolithic or early Bronze Age. Its homeland is the subject of competing hypotheses. The academic consensus supports the Kurgan hypothesis, which places it on the Pontic–Caspian steppe, in what is now Ukraine and southern Russia, in association with the Yamnaya culture.

The oldest records are isolated Hittite words and names in Assyrian texts from Kültepe in eastern Anatolia, dating to the 20th century BCE. The Anitta text, in Hittite, dated to 1700 BCE, is the oldest known text in an Indo-European language, and fragmentary Mycenaean Greek records date from between 1450 and 1350 BCE. How the parent language split into its branches is not attested, and the timeline is disputed: David Anthony places Pre-Anatolian at about 4200 BCE and Proto-Indo-Iranian at about 2200 BCE.

European visitors to the Indian subcontinent began to notice similarities among Indo-Aryan, Iranian and European languages in the 16th century. In 1583 the Jesuit Thomas Stephens wrote from Goa of likenesses between North Indian languages and Greek and Latin, and in 1585 the merchant Filippo Sassetti compared Sanskrit and Italian words, such as sapta and sette for seven. Neither led to further inquiry. In 1647 the Dutch scholar Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn proposed a common ancestor that he called Scythian.

In 1786 Sir William Jones told the Asiatic Society of Bengal that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin bore a stronger affinity than could have arisen by accident and had sprung from some common source which perhaps no longer existed. The analysis of these relationships and the reconstruction of their common source were central to the development of historical linguistics as a discipline in the 19th century. The current consensus accepts no genetic link between the family and any other language family.
indonesia: Indonesia is an equatorial archipelago of coastal plains, mountains and volcanic islands, extending 5,120 kilometres from east to west across three time zones and 1,760 kilometres from north to south. Published counts of its islands range from 13,000 to 25,000, and the most widely cited official count is 17,508, with about 6,000 inhabited.

Its five main islands are Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, Borneo and New Guinea. Strategic shipping routes between the Indian and Pacific oceans run through the Malacca, Sunda and Lombok straits. The country lies on a complex plate-boundary zone, with at least 127 active volcanoes and a high exposure to earthquakes and tsunamis; the Toba super-eruption about 74,000 years ago was one of the largest known.

Java has yielded hominin fossils generally attributed to Homo erectus, and narrative cave art in Sulawesi has been dated to a minimum age of 51,200 years. From the third millennium BCE Austronesian-speaking communities moved south from Taiwan through the Philippines into the archipelago, and from around 500 BCE regional trading networks connected it with South and East Asia.

In the early centuries CE some coastal communities in Borneo, Sumatra and Java developed into trading ports, and Indian merchants and religious specialists brought Sanskrit literacy, Hindu and Buddhist practices and models of kingship that local rulers adopted. Srivijaya, founded in southeastern Sumatra in the late 7th century, became a maritime trading polity and a centre of Buddhist learning.

Rulers in central Java supported the building of Borobudur and Prambanan between the 8th and 10th centuries. Majapahit emerged in eastern Java in the late 13th century after Raden Wijaya used a Mongol expedition to defeat his rivals and then forced the Mongols to withdraw.

Its rulers claimed suzerainty over ports across the archipelago, although beyond Java this authority was often exercised indirectly through tributary, ritual and commercial relationships. Islamic states grew from the late medieval period, and European powers competed to monopolise trade in the Spice Islands of Maluku. Dutch commercial and colonial control expanded from the 17th century and covered most of the archipelago by the early 20th century.

Indonesia proclaimed its independence in the aftermath of World War II. After the fall of Suharto in 1998, decentralisation transferred substantial lawmaking powers to provincial, regency and city governments, and constitutional amendments between 1999 and 2002 introduced direct presidential elections, which began in 2004. The country is a presidential republic of 38 provinces.

The Javanese are the largest ethnic group, at about 40%. More than 700 languages are spoken, and Indonesian, a standardised variety of Malay adopted as a language of unity through the 1928 Youth Pledge, is the official language. Its motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, comes from the 14th-century poem Sutasoma.
indus: The Indus is 3,180 kilometres long. It rises in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, where it is known as Sengge Zangbo, flows northwest through Ladakh and Gilgit-Baltistan, and bends sharply to the left after the Nanga Parbat massif. It then runs south-by-southwest through Pakistan and empties into the Arabian Sea near Karachi. Its left-bank tributary on the plains is the Panjnad, formed by the successive confluences of the five Punjab rivers: the Chenab, Jhelum, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. Its principal right-bank tributaries are the Shyok, Gilgit, Kabul, Kurram and Gomal.

Its headwaters, with those of the Yarlung Tsangpo to the east, follow the suture where the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate about 50 million years ago. Its traditional name in Sanskrit and Tibetan is Sindhu, a word for river, and the English name derives through Greek and Old Persian from the same root, as do Hindustan and India.

The cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, date back to around 3300 BCE and were among the largest human settlements of the ancient world. The civilisation reached from northeast Afghanistan to Pakistan and northwest India, and over 1,052 cities and settlements have been found, mainly around the Ghaggar-Hakra River and its tributaries; only about 40 sites lie on the Indus and its tributaries. Its people were the first to build irrigation canals in the valley, and the Kushan and Mughal empires later built canals too.

In the 2nd millennium BCE the Punjab was called Sapta Sindhu in the Rigveda and Hapta Həndu in the Avesta, both meaning seven rivers. Early kingdoms of the valley included Gandhāra and Sindhu-Sauvīra. The river became known to the western world when King Darius of Persia sent his Greek subject Scylax of Caryanda to explore it, about 515 BCE. In 1850 the British East India Company introduced modern irrigation and restored old canals, and the British supervised the building of one of the most complex irrigation networks in the world.

The Indus is the chief supplier of water to the plains of Punjab and Sindh, where rainfall is meagre, and it is the backbone of agriculture in Pakistan. The river is sacred to Hindus, and the Sindhu Darshan Festival is held on its banks at Leh. The Indus River dolphin is found only in this river.
industrial-revolution: Several factors enabled industrialisation: high agricultural productivity, as in the British Agricultural Revolution, which supplied surplus labour and food; managerial and entrepreneurial skills; ports, rivers, canals and roads that moved raw materials and goods cheaply; natural resources such as coal, iron and waterfalls; political stability and a legal system that supported business; and capital available to invest. Innovations such as Jethro Tull's seed drill of 1701 and Andrew Meikle's threshing machine of 1784 cut the labour that farming required. Before the change, most manufacturing took place in China and India, and India, China and parts of the Middle East produced most of the world's cotton cloth.

The textile industry was the first to use modern production methods. In 1750 Britain imported 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton, mostly spun and woven by hand in Lancashire homes and workshops. By 1787 raw cotton consumption was 22 million pounds, most of it spun on machines, and in 1800 the industry used 52 million pounds. Mechanised spinning powered by water and later steam raised output per worker by a factor of around 500, and the power loom by a factor of 40.

Coke replaced charcoal in iron making: in 1720 Britain made 20,500 tons of charcoal iron and 400 tons with coke, and in 1806 coke cast iron reached 250,000 tons. John Roebuck's lead chamber process of 1746 began large-scale chemical production. Steam supplied an estimated 10,000 horsepower in Britain by 1800 and 210,000 by 1815, though water and wind supplied most industrial power early on. William Murdoch's gas lighting reached London between 1812 and 1820, and steam locomotives came in the early 19th century. Mechanised production spread to continental Europe and the United States by about 1840.

Historians debate the precise start and end of the Industrial Revolution and the pace of its changes. Growth slowed from the late 1830s as markets for the early innovations matured, and revived after 1870 with the steel-making, assembly-line and electrical innovations of the Second Industrial Revolution. The earliest recorded use of the term Industrial Revolution was in 1799, by the French envoy Louis-Guillaume Otto, and Arnold Toynbee's lectures of 1881 are credited with popularising it.

Output and population grew at unprecedented rates. Visible poverty, a growing population and new wealth caused tensions between rich and poor, which led to ideas such as socialism, communism and anarchism. Children as young as eight worked in textile mills. Economists such as Robert Lucas Jr. hold that for the first time the living standards of ordinary people began sustained growth, while others say they did not improve meaningfully until the 20th century. After the Industrial Revolution most manufacturing took place in North America and Western Europe.
international-monetary-fund: During the Great Depression countries sharply raised barriers to trade in an attempt to improve their failing economies. This led to the devaluation of national currencies and a decline in world trade, and the breakdown of international monetary cooperation created a need for oversight. Representatives of 45 governments met at the Bretton Woods Conference in the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to discuss a framework for postwar international economic cooperation and how to rebuild Europe. The Fund was established there in July 1944, on the ideas of Harry Dexter White and John Maynard Keynes.

For its first three decades the Fund oversaw the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rate arrangements. Countries that joined between 1945 and 1971 agreed to keep their exchange rates at levels that could be adjusted only to correct a fundamental disequilibrium in the balance of payments, and only with the Fund's agreement. Special drawing rights, created in 1969, were each worth 0.888671 grams of gold, roughly one US dollar at the time.

After the Bretton Woods agreement was terminated in 1971, the Fund redefined the unit in 1973 as the value of a selection of world currencies, and its role shifted to managing balance-of-payments difficulties and international financial crises. In the early 2000s it provided two major lending packages, to Argentina and to Uruguay.

The Fund is a specialised agency of the United Nations, headquartered in Washington, D.C., and acts as a lender of last resort to members facing balance of payments crises. Through a quota system, countries contribute funds to a pool from which they can borrow, and a country's quota also determines its voting power. Each member has basic votes equal to 5.502% of the total, plus one additional vote for each 100,000 special drawing rights of its quota.

A managing director, who has historically been European, leads the staff, and the first deputy has by convention been a citizen of the United States. Conditionality, the policies the Fund requires in exchange for its financial resources, was introduced in a 1952 decision of the Executive Board. Critics argue that these conditions impose austerity and limit the economic sovereignty of borrowing nations, and that the Fund's governance is dominated by Western countries.
iran: Iran has an area of 1,648,195 square kilometres, the sixth-largest country entirely in Asia. It is one of the world's most mountainous countries, consisting mostly of the Iranian Plateau, with ranges such as the Zagros and Alborz in the populous west. Mount Damavand, at 5,610 metres, is the highest point and the highest volcano in Asia. Lush Caspian Hyrcanian forests cover the north, while the east is mostly desert basins such as the Kavir and Lut deserts. The country lies in a seismically active area, where an earthquake of magnitude 7.0 or higher occurs on average once every ten years.

Hominins were present in Iran around 800,000 years ago, and agriculture appeared some 12,000 years ago; Ganj Dareh shows the earliest known domestication of goats, around 10,000 years ago. Susa, later the capital of Elam, was first settled in 4400–4200 BCE, and Elam lasted from 3200 to 539 BCE. The earliest Iranian peoples began to arrive from Central Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE. The Median dynasty ruled the earliest Iranian state, and in 612 BCE Cyaxares and the Babylonian king Nabopolassar destroyed Nineveh. Cyrus the Great then defeated the Medes and founded the Achaemenid Empire, the largest-ever Iranian state, and his son Cambyses II conquered Egypt.

Alexander the Great conquered the empire in the 4th century BCE, the Parthian Empire arose in the 3rd century BCE, and the Sasanian Empire succeeded it in the 3rd century CE. After the 7th-century Muslim conquest Iran underwent Islamization, and during the Iranian Intermezzo Iranian Muslim dynasties ended Arab rule and revived the Persian language. Seljuk and Khwarazmian rule, Mongol conquests and the Timurid Renaissance followed. In the 16th century the Safavid dynasty re-established a unified Iranian state with Twelver Shia Islam as its official religion. Iran was a leading world power under the Afsharid Empire but lost the status after the Qajars took power in the 1790s.

Reza Shah founded the Pahlavi dynasty after ousting the last Qajar Shah in 1925. The Iranian Revolution of 1979 overthrew the monarchy, and Ruhollah Khomeini became the first supreme leader of the Islamic Republic; Iraq invaded in 1980, starting an eight-year war. The supreme leader is head of state and commands the armed forces, while the president has limited power. Tehran, with about 9.4 million people, is the capital and largest city. Persians are estimated at 51% of the population and Azerbaijanis at 24% in a 2003 estimate, although ethnic composition is debated because no state censuses count it. Iran has 30 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
iraq: Iraq lies in West Asia, bordered by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Iran, Kuwait, Jordan and Syria, with a coastline of 58 kilometres on the northern Persian Gulf. The Tigris and Euphrates run south through the country into the Shatt al-Arab and then the Persian Gulf. Fertile alluvial plains lie between and beside the two rivers, which carry about 60,000,000 cubic metres of silt a year to the delta, and marshlands flank the estuary.

Rocky deserts cover about 40 percent of Iraq and another 30 percent is mountainous, with the northwestern end of the Zagros range. Summer temperatures average above 40 °C for most of the country, and most places receive less than 250 millimetres of rain a year.

Iraq largely coincides with ancient Mesopotamia. Sumer emerged between 6000 and 5000 BCE during the Neolithic Ubaid period, and is recognised as the world's earliest civilisation. The territory includes the heartlands of the Akkadian, Neo-Sumerian, Babylonian, Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian empires. After the Achaemenid conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, Cyrus the Great adopted titles such as King of Babylon and King of Sumer and Akkad, and Aramaic became the lingua franca of the empire.

Babylon surrendered without resistance to Alexander the Great in 331 BCE, and after his death in 323 BCE Seleucia became the imperial capital in Mesopotamia. Cuneiform writing and temple institutions continued under Seleucid rule. After the Arab conquest in the 7th century, Iraq became the centre of the Abbasid Caliphate, and the name Iraq came into use for the region. The Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258, and from the 16th century until the 20th Iraq was governed within the Ottoman system.

Iraq became independent in 1932. A military coup led by Abdul Karim Qasim overthrew the monarchy in 1958, and the Ba'ath Party took power in 1968. The country fought a war with Iran from 1980 to 1988, invaded Kuwait in 1990, and was invaded by a U.S.-led coalition in 2003. Iraq is a federal parliamentary republic.

Oil was nationalised in 1972. The 2021 population estimate was 43,533,592, and most Iraqis are Arabs, with Kurds, Turkmens, Assyrians, Yazidis and others. Arabic and Kurdish are the official languages.
iron-age: The Iron Age is the final epoch of the three-age system of technology, after the Stone Age and the Bronze Age. The concept was devised for Iron Age Europe and the ancient Near East. Meteoric iron had been used for thousands of years earlier; the earliest known artifacts are nine small beads dated to 3200 BCE from burials at Gerzeh in Lower Egypt.

The beginning of the Iron Age is defined locally by archaeological convention, when smelted iron, especially steel tools and weapons, replaces bronze in common use. Smelting iron requires temperatures above 1,250 °C, impractical to reach commonly until the end of the second millennium BCE, and it also required procedures for removing impurities and regulating carbon content.

The three-age system was first used for the archaeology of Europe in the first half of the 19th century and was introduced to Scandinavia by Christian Jürgensen Thomsen in the 1830s; its name recalls Hesiod's Ages of Man. The earliest tentative evidence for iron-making is a few iron fragments with suitable carbon content from Proto-Hittite layers at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Turkey, dated to 2200 to 2000 BCE. A long-held view that a Hittite monopoly on ironworking underlay Hittite success no longer represents scholarly consensus.

Modern evidence identifies the start of large-scale global iron production about 1200 BCE, which marks the end of the Bronze Age. Anthony Snodgrass suggests that a shortage of tin and disrupted Mediterranean trade about 1300 BCE forced metalworkers to look for an alternative; once tin returned, iron was cheaper, stronger and lighter.

The Iron Age varies by region. In the ancient Near East it is considered to last from about 1200 BCE, the Bronze Age collapse, to about 550 BCE, with the Achaemenid Empire traditionally the end date. Iron working spread through the Mediterranean and to South Asia between the 12th and 11th centuries BCE. In Central and Western Europe the Iron Age lasted from about 800 BCE to about 1 BCE, ending with Roman conquest, and in Northern Europe it began about the 5th century BCE.

In China, writing developed first, so Bronze Age China passes almost directly into the Qin dynasty. Many parts of Africa passed directly from stone to iron, and some archaeologists believe iron metallurgy developed independently in sub-Saharan Africa; the Nok culture may have smelted iron from about 1000 BCE. Indigenous cultures of the Americas did not develop an iron economy before European contact.
isaac-newton: Isaac Newton was born on 25 December 1642 (4 January 1643 in the modern calendar) at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire. His father, also named Isaac Newton, had died three months before. Born prematurely, he was a small child; his mother, Hannah Ayscough, said that he could have fit inside a quart mug. When he was three she remarried and left him in the care of his grandmother. From about the age of twelve until seventeen he attended The King's School in Grantham. His mother tried to make him a farmer, an occupation he hated, until his uncle and the schoolmaster persuaded her to send him back to school.

Newton was a fellow of Trinity College and the second Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge, appointed at the age of 26. He refused to take holy orders in the Church of England. He served two brief terms as Member of Parliament for the University of Cambridge, in 1689 to 1690 and 1701 to 1702.

In 1696 he moved to London as Warden of the Mint, a post obtained through the patronage of Charles Montagu, 1st Earl of Halifax. He took charge of England's great recoining. He became Master of the Mint in 1699, holding the post for the last 30 years of his life. These appointments were intended as sinecures, but Newton took them seriously, reforming the currency and punishing clippers and counterfeiters. He was president of the Royal Society from 1703 and was knighted by Queen Anne in 1705. He died on 31 March 1727, at the age of 84, and was the first scientist to be buried at Westminster Abbey.

Newton began his work on calculus, which he called fluxions, in 1664, and by 1665 had developed a systematic calculus unifying differentiation and integration. He was self-taught in mathematics. He later quarrelled with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz over priority. Both are now credited with developing calculus independently, though Newton came to it much earlier. Leibniz's notation, however, proved the more convenient. The Principia of 1687 set out his laws of motion and universal gravitation, and his Opticks appeared in 1704.

Newton was a devout but heterodox Christian who privately rejected the doctrine of the Trinity, and he devoted much time to biblical chronology and alchemy. Of an estimated ten million words in his papers, about one million deal with alchemy. Most of his writing in these fields stayed unpublished until long after his death. His library of 1,752 identified books held 477 on theology and 169 on alchemy.
islam: According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad was born in Mecca in 570 CE and was orphaned early. He grew up as a trader, became known as the 'trusted one' and later married his employer, the businesswoman Khadija. In 610 CE he retreated to the Cave of Hira near Mecca, where he is said to have received the first revelation of the Quran from the angel Gabriel, an event known as the Night of Power. Over the next 22 years he continued to receive revelations.

In Mecca he preached first in secret and then in public, urging his listeners to abandon polytheism. Many early converts were women, the poor, foreigners and slaves such as the first muezzin, Bilal ibn Rabah al-Habashi. The Meccan elite felt he was destabilizing their social order, and they profited from pilgrimages to the idols of the Kaaba. By the time of his death most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted, and Muslim rule then expanded outside Arabia under the Rashidun Caliphate.

The Islamic creed requires belief in six articles: God, angels, revelation, prophets, the Day of Resurrection and divine predestination. The central concept is tawhid, the oneness of God, and associating anything with God is idolatry, called shirk. Muslims consider the Quran the verbatim word of God and hold Muhammad to be the final prophet. His teachings and example, the Sunnah, are documented in hadith. Islam has no clergy in the sacerdotal sense, and no intermediaries are needed to reach God.

Five acts of worship are duties: the shahada, the declaration of faith; the five daily prayers, recited in Arabic and performed toward the Kaaba; almsgiving (zakat); fasting during Ramadan; and the pilgrimage (hajj) to Mecca. The two main festivals are Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

The two main branches are Sunni Islam, 87–90% of Muslims, and Shia Islam, 10–13%. The divide began in disagreement over the succession to Muhammad and grew to cover theology and law. Sunnis follow one of four schools of jurisprudence: Hanafi, Hanbali, Maliki or Shafi'i. Sharia, the body of religious law, is studied through fiqh. Sufism, a mystical approach seeking direct personal experience of God, is not a sect, and its adherents belong to various denominations. About 25.6% of the global population, roughly 2 billion people, are Muslims. They are a majority in 53 countries, and about 12% live in Indonesia.
islamabad: Islamabad lies about 540 metres above sea level at the northern edge of the Pothohar Plateau, at the foot of the Margalla Hills, in the northern part of the Punjab region. It forms a conurbation with the older Gakhar city of Rawalpindi, to its south; the two are commonly called the Twin Cities. The city is 120 km southwest of Muzaffarabad, 185 km east of Peshawar and 295 km northwest of Lahore. It covers 906 square kilometres, and a further Specified Area of 2,717 square kilometres runs into the hills. The southern part is an undulating plain drained by the Kurang River, on which the Rawal Dam stands.

The Pothohar Plateau is considered one of the earliest sites of human settlement in Asia. Stone Age artefacts dating from 100,000 to 500,000 years ago have been found there, among them rudimentary stones from the terraces of the Soan River. Excavations by Abdul Ghafoor Lone found relics and human skulls dating back to 5000 BCE, which indicate Neolithic peoples on the banks of the Soan, who later formed small communities around 3000 BCE. Remnants of Aryan, Soanian and Indus Valley cultures, and Buddhist remains, can still be found in the region.

Later buildings include Pharwala Fort, built by the Gakhars in the 15th century, and Rawat Fort of the 16th century, which holds the grave of their chief Sultan Sarang Khan. The Mughal commander Raja Man Singh turned the village of Saidpur into a place of Hindu worship and built ponds there, and the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb built the shrine of Bari Imam. The modern city was built as a planned capital in the 1960s and established in 1967, replacing Karachi. The Greek architect Constantinos Apostolou Doxiadis drew up its master plan, which divided the city into eight zones: administrative, commercial, educational, industrial, diplomatic, residential, rural and green.

The name means City of Islam, from the Arabic Islam and the Persian suffix -abad. Residential sectors are each identified by a letter and a number and cover about 2 km by 2 km. The city is administered federally as the Islamabad Capital Territory, and its parks and forests include Margalla Hills National Park and Shakarparian. The Faisal Mosque, completed in 1986 to a design by the Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, was named after King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz of Saudi Arabia, who financed it, and can hold up to 74,000 worshippers. The Islamabad Museum holds relics of the Gandhara period.
istanbul: Istanbul straddles the Bosporus Strait in north-western Turkey, between the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea. The strait is the only passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean. About two-thirds of the population live on the European side and the rest in Asia. The meeting of the Sea of Marmara, the Bosporus and the Golden Horn gave the city both a defence against attack and a natural toll-gate for trade. The belief that seven hills make up the city is a myth: there are more than 50 hills within its limits.

Neolithic artefacts show that the historic peninsula was settled as far back as the 6th millennium BCE. Megarian colonists founded Byzantium around 657 BCE, claiming descent from its founder Byzas, said to be the son of the god Poseidon and the nymph Ceroëssa. The Roman emperor Constantine the Great refounded the city in 324 CE, at first calling it New Rome, and it became Constantinople in 330.

For nearly 16 centuries it served as the capital of four empires: the Roman Empire from 330 to 395, the Byzantine Empire from 395 to 1204 and from 1261 to 1453, the Latin Empire from 1204 to 1261, and the Ottoman Empire from 1453 to 1922. It was important in the advance of Christianity in Roman and Byzantine times. The Ottomans conquered it in 1453 and made it the seat of their caliphate. By 500 CE it had 400,000 to 500,000 people, more than Rome, and it was the largest city in Europe from 1500 to 1750, when London surpassed it. Constantinople remained the usual Western name until the 1930s. The Republic of Turkey made Ankara its capital in 1923.

Istanbul is the largest city in Turkey, with a population of over 15 million. The historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and palaces and imperial mosques still line its hills. The Galata Tower is the one survivor of the medieval Genoese fortifications of Galata. The first Turkish newspaper, Takvim-i Vekayi, was published there in 1831.
isthmian-games: The games were reputed to have begun as funeral games for Melicertes, instituted by Sisyphus, the legendary king of Corinth, who found the body and buried it on the Isthmus. Another myth, probably later, held that Theseus, the legendary king of Athens, enlarged a closed night rite into athletic games dedicated to Poseidon and open to all Greeks. A further version credits Kypselos, tyrant of Corinth in the 7th century BCE, with restoring the games to their old splendour. According to Solinus they were constituted in the 49th Olympiad; 582 BCE is the date generally accepted, though one recent study places the first games in 581 BCE.

The festival was held in spring, in the second and fourth years of each Olympiad, the year before and the year after the Olympic Games, at the rural sanctuary of Poseidon on the Isthmus of Corinth, a place easily reached by land and by sea. The contests were the same as at Olympia, among them wrestling, boxing, pankration and horse and chariot racing, and there were musical and poetical contests in which women were allowed to compete.

Until at least the 5th century BCE, the time of Pindar, the victor's wreath was of celery; later it was made of pine. A victor might also be honoured with a statue or an ode, and Athens paid its own victors 100 drachmas. Before the games Corinth declared a truce that gave athletes safe passage through Greece: in 412 BCE the Athenians were invited as usual although Athens and Corinth were at war. The games were especially popular with Athenians, while the Eleans boycotted them.

The festival served many as a forum for political propaganda, and from 228 or 229 BCE Romans were allowed to take part. Corinth, rebuilt by Caesar in 44 BCE, recovered the games shortly afterwards, but they were then held in the city itself and did not return to the Isthmus until 42 or 43 CE. Libanius mentions cult activity at the Isthmus into the middle of the 4th century, and the games probably continued at least until the end of that century. The circumstances of their end are unknown; imperial pressure against pagan rites grew at that time, though some polytheistic cult practices continued at Corinth into the 6th century.
italy: Italy consists of the Italian Peninsula, which extends into the Mediterranean Sea, together with Sicily, Sardinia and nearly 800 islands. It covers 301,340 square kilometres, with the Alps along most of its northern boundary and the Apennine Mountains forming the backbone of the peninsula. Over 35% of its territory is mountainous, and the highest point is the summit of Mont Blanc at 4,810 metres. Many parts are of volcanic origin, and active volcanoes include Mount Etna in Sicily, the largest in Europe, as well as Vulcano, Stromboli and Vesuvius. The sovereign states of San Marino and Vatican City are enclaves within Italy.

Lower Paleolithic artefacts dating back 850,000 years have been recovered from Monte Poggiolo. Pre-Roman Italy was inhabited mostly by Italic peoples, along with the Etruscans, the Elymians and Sicani of Sicily, and the prehistoric Sardinians who gave rise to the Nuragic civilisation. Phoenicians established emporiums on the coasts of Sicily and Sardinia, and during the 8th and 7th centuries BCE Greek colonies were founded, an area later known as Magna Graecia. Rome, a settlement on the River Tiber traditionally founded in 753 BCE, was ruled by monarchs for 244 years, and in 509 BCE the Romans expelled the monarchy and established a republic.

Roman expansion consolidated the peninsula, named Italia, and Rome grew into an empire stretching from Britain to the borders of Persia. Augustus, the first emperor, began an age of peace and prosperity. Barbarian invasions led to the decline and fall of the Western Roman Empire, after which the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy was created.

By the 11th century Italian city-states and maritime republics expanded, and the Italian Renaissance flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries. After centuries of political division the Kingdom of Italy was established in 1861, following wars of independence and the Expedition of the Thousand. The fascist dictatorship was established in 1922, and in 1946 a republic replaced the monarchy.

Italy has 58,915,561 inhabitants, and Rome is the capital. It has been a unitary parliamentary republic since 1946, with a president elected for a single seven-year term and a perfectly bicameral Parliament made up of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate of the Republic.
From the late 19th century to the 1960s Italy was a country of mass emigration, and the diaspora included more than 25 million Italians. Italy has 62 World Heritage Sites.
ivory-coast: Portuguese merchant-explorers of the 15th and 16th centuries divided the west coast of Africa into four coasts named for the trade each offered. The Costa do Marfim, translated into French as Côte d'Ivoire, took its name from the export of ivory, as the Gold Coast and the Slave Coast did from theirs. Other names for the stretch included the Côte de Dents, the Coast of Teeth, and the Windward Coast. In the 19th century usage settled on Côte d'Ivoire, a name kept through French rule and independence in 1960.

The first human presence is hard to determine, since remains are poorly preserved in the humid climate, though polished axes and tool fragments suggest a large presence in the Upper Paleolithic period or at least the Neolithic. Historians believe the earliest inhabitants were displaced or absorbed by the ancestors of the present peoples, who migrated south into the area before the 16th century.

The first recorded history comes from the chronicles of Berber traders, who ran a caravan trade across the Sahara in salt, slaves and gold. Around the southern terminals of those routes, Djenné, Gao and Timbuktu, the great Sudanic empires developed, and they also became centres of Islamic education. From the 11th century Islam spread south into the north of what is now Ivory Coast. The Ghana Empire flourished between the 4th and 13th centuries, and the Mali Empire that followed held only the northwest corner of Ivory Coast, around Odienné.

The country was traditionally home to several states, including Gyaaman, the Kong Empire and Baoulé. It became a protectorate of France in 1843 and was consolidated as a French colony in 1893 during the Scramble for Africa. It achieved independence in 1960 under Félix Houphouët-Boigny, who ruled until 1993. Through coffee and cocoa production it became an economic powerhouse in West Africa in the 1960s and 1970s. The capital has been Yamoussoukro since 1983.

Ivory Coast is a republic with strong executive power vested in its president, and its parliament consists of a Senate and a National Assembly. Since 2011 it has been organised into 12 districts and two autonomous cities. French is the official language and about 78 languages are spoken, among them Baoulé, Dyula and Bété. The citizen population falls into macroethnic groupings, chiefly the Akan, Voltaic or Gur peoples, Northern Mandés, Kru-speaking peoples and Southern Mandés. Each ethnic group has its own music, mostly with strong vocal polyphony, and talking drums and polyrhythms are common.
